analysis.one_liner: Wipes out the FCC's open internet rules that stop broadband providers from blocking or slowing web traffic.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 37 House Republicans, never got a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have voided the Federal Communications Commission's 2010 Open Internet order — the rules commonly called net neutrality — and barred the FCC from reissuing them or anything substantially similar unless a new law authorized it. Those rules stopped broadband and cable companies from blocking websites, slowing traffic, or playing favorites among online services. The bill kept narrow exceptions for national security, public safety, and law enforcement. It never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband and cable internet providers like Comcast, Verizon, and AT&T. The bill would have freed them from the FCC's rules against blocking or discriminating among web traffic, letting them manage their networks as they saw fit and, under the general business models of the industry, charge websites and services for faster delivery or slow rivals' traffic.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that the FCC's 2010 Open Internet order 'shall have no force or effect' and that the FCC may not reissue it or anything substantially similar unless Congress passes a new law authorizing it.
The bill leaves the FCC free to issue rules only for national security, public safety, or law enforcement purposes — everything else in the open internet rules would be off limits.
It was introduced by Rep. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee with 37 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

analysis.who_pays: Internet users, and the websites and online services they rely on. The rules being voided are what prevented internet providers from blocking sites, slowing service, or charging web companies extra to reach customers at full speed — costs that would ultimately flow to consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill's only carve-outs are for national security, public safety, and law enforcement; it offers no replacement consumer protections against blocking, throttling, or paid favoritism of web traffic.

Supporters argued the FCC lacked clear legal authority for the 2010 rules — a federal court had already struck down part of them in January 2014 — and that the rules deterred network investment. The bill's answer was to eliminate the rules outright rather than write new statutory protections, leaving no enforceable guarantee of an open internet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go entirely to a small set of large internet providers, while the costs fall on everyone who uses the internet, whose access to sites and services would depend on their provider's business choices. The bill is not a compromise: it removes existing protections and replaces them with nothing, requiring a future act of Congress before any open internet rule could return.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2014 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Communications Subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced the Internet Freedom Act on February 21, 2014, joined by 37 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and to the Communications and Technology Subcommittee on February 28, 2014.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a markup or a vote in either chamber and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet users came out ahead: the FCC's open internet rules, though narrowed by the courts, remained on the books, and broadband providers did not get the deregulation the bill offered.

for.name: Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void the FCC's 2010 open internet rules.

for.name: Major broadband and cable providers
for.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the FCC's open internet rules and backed legislative efforts to repeal them.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over telecommunications law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Communications Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor — 38 members in all — was a House Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-run committee.

industries.note: The bill would have wiped out the FCC rules that barred these companies from blocking websites, slowing traffic, or discriminating among online services. Their gain was directly the public's loss: users would have no enforceable guarantee of equal access to the internet.

industries.industry: Online content and streaming companies (edge providers)
industries.note: These companies — video streaming, search, e-commerce, and small web businesses — are protected by open internet rules from being charged for priority delivery or slowed relative to competitors. The bill's repeal of those rules would have exposed them to exactly those tactics.
